listeningParts.title: Booking a beginner pottery course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A customer calls a pottery studio about an introductory course.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Hello, Brookfield Pottery Studio. This is Alice at reception. If you're asking about collecting finished work, that happens on Saturday mornings, but I can also help with course bookings. What would you like to know?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'd like to book a beginner course for myself and my cousin. Neither of us has done any pottery before. We saw photographs of people using wheels on your website, but we're not sure whether that is the best place to start. We'd like to make something we can actually keep.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We offer a wheel introduction and a hand-building course. For people who want a first finished object, I'd recommend hand-building. You begin with a small bowl, and later you can try a box or a simple vase. The wheel course is more about learning a movement than completing several pieces immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Then hand-building sounds right. I noticed two prices online, sixty-eight pounds and eighty-two pounds. Does the higher price mean that materials are included, or is it a longer course? I couldn't find that information on the page I was looking at.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Sixty-eight pounds is the old price from last term. The current fee is eighty-two pounds per person for four sessions. That includes clay, shared tools and the finishing of two pieces. If you make additional work and want it finished, there may be an extra charge, which the tutor explains before you decide.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thank you. We'd rather know that beforehand. Is the class on Tuesday evenings? My cousin works late on Thursdays, and we would like to attend together rather than join different groups.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Tuesday is the advanced group. The beginner course runs on Wednesday, from six thirty until eight thirty. The first session is on the ninth. Please arrive fifteen minutes early that evening so we can complete the registration and show you where to put your belongings.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wednesday works for both of us. Do we need to bring special equipment? I've got an old apron, but I don't own any pottery tools. I wouldn't want to spend a lot before knowing whether I enjoy the course.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You don't need to buy tools. Bring your apron and a towel for your hands. Wear clothes that you don't mind getting marked, and shoes that cover your feet. We don't recommend bringing jewellery to the worktables. There are lockers near reception, but people sometimes forget what they have put in them.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: All right. My cousin has difficulty standing for a long time. Would the course still be suitable? The pictures show some people standing, but perhaps they were only watching a demonstration.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Most of the work can be done seated, and the tutor can arrange a lower table. Please mention that on the registration form, so it is ready when you arrive. The classroom is on the ground floor, with a separate entrance from the courtyard. You won't need to use the stairs to the exhibition room.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's helpful. Could you put the booking in my name? I'm Miriam Hensley. That's H-E-N-S-L-E-Y. I'll pay for both places now if that is possible, and my cousin can pay me back.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Certainly, Miriam. I'll send a payment link rather than take card details on the telephone. Please complete it within two days. Until then, the places will be held for you. Once payment is received, you'll get a confirmation email and the registration form for each person.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what happens to the pieces after the last session? We live outside town, so it would be useful to know whether we'll have to make a separate journey to collect them.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: They won't be ready to take home that evening. Allow three weeks after the course for finishing. We will email when they are ready. Collect them from the shop, not reception, because that is where finished student work is stored. The shop staff will ask for your name and the course date.

listeningParts.title: Visiting a working craft centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces the rooms and activities at a public craft centre.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Welcome to the Lantern Craft Centre. The building used to be a storage depot, but the rooms now support several different kinds of making. It is important to remember that some people here are at work rather than taking part in a demonstration. Please look for the open-door symbol before entering a room, and do not assume that an unlocked door is an invitation to walk in.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The first place to visit is the materials room. This is not a shop. You can handle labelled samples of clay, wood and other materials, and compare them with examples of finished objects. The intention is to show that choosing a material involves more than liking its colour. A maker may also think about weight, the way a surface feels and how an object will be used. Children are welcome, but an adult should stay with them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next is the demonstration room. There is a programme of short talks throughout the day. You don't need a ticket for the talks, but the room has limited seating, so arriving early is sensible. The maker will usually pause for questions at the end, rather than answer while handling tools. Please wait for that invitation. A demonstration is a chance to see part of a process; it should not be taken as enough training to repeat specialist work unsupervised.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The gallery takes a different approach. Instead of showing only finished pieces, it displays drawings, early attempts and revised designs beside them. We hope visitors will see that changes are part of making, not evidence that a maker failed to plan. Some objects were altered because the first version was awkward to hold. Others changed because a material did not behave as expected. The labels explain the particular decision rather than presenting every change as a general rule.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: At the far end is the handling collection. This is the one area where you may pick up finished examples, but please remain at the table and follow the volunteer's guidance. The objects have been selected for handling; gallery pieces have not. If you are uncertain which collection an object belongs to, ask. We would rather answer a simple question than have someone copy what they saw another visitor doing in a different room.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: For people who would like to try an activity, the afternoon workshop is making a small paper structure. It does not involve the specialist equipment used in the studios. Book at the desk beside the stairs. The workshop is included in your admission, but you need a separate place reservation. Only reserve for people who will actually take part. Parents watching a child do not need a participant's place.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: There are two changes to today's leaflet. The talk about preparing an exhibition will be in the library, because the usual meeting room is being repaired. Also, the café will close at four, half an hour earlier than the centre. Food and drink must stay in the café or the courtyard. Even a covered cup can spill, so please don't carry one into the handling collection.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you want information about commissioning work, leave your details at the information desk. The volunteer there can explain how to contact a maker, but cannot promise a price or completion date on their behalf. Each project needs discussion of its own requirements. Buying an object from the shop is different: the price on its label is the price you pay, and you can usually take it home that day.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, photography is permitted in the public displays where a camera symbol is shown. Flash is not allowed anywhere in the centre. Please ask before photographing a working maker, and keep the passageways clear while taking pictures. If you need somewhere quiet, the reading corner is available beside the library. You can return to any of the public rooms later; there is no required order once this introduction is finished.

listeningParts.title: Planning a comparison of drinking-cup handles
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two design students discuss the scope and method of a supervised classroom project.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Before you make the final models, tell me what your handle project is meant to investigate. Last time, you had a very broad idea about designing the perfect cup. That would involve far more questions than you can answer in a short classroom exercise.

dialogue.speaker: Leah
dialogue.text: We've narrowed it to the space between the handle and the side of the cup. We want to compare how easy it is for volunteers to put their fingers through that space. We're not trying to test a finished drinking product, and we won't use hot liquid or ask anyone to lift a heavy load.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: The models will be light and unfilled. We first considered changing both the shape and the gap, but that would make the comparison difficult to interpret. Now the overall handle shape will stay the same, and we'll vary the gap. The tutor in the model workshop has agreed to check the pieces before volunteers handle them.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That is a clearer question. How will you make sure that what you ask volunteers to do is consistent? A person who has already tried several versions may approach the next one differently from someone seeing the task for the first time.

dialogue.speaker: Leah
dialogue.text: We'll write a short instruction and use the same wording each time. We also want to vary the order of the models, rather than always showing the smallest gap first. Otherwise, a response to the later model might partly reflect getting familiar with the activity.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: We're going to record what people actually do as well as their comments. If someone says a model is comfortable but changes their grip several times, that difference is worth noting. It doesn't automatically prove that their comment is wrong, though. We should ask what they meant instead of replacing their account with our interpretation.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And think about your sample. A few classmates will give you useful observations, but they won't represent everyone who uses a cup. Describe who took part without collecting more personal information than the assignment needs.

dialogue.speaker: Leah
dialogue.text: We'll recruit volunteers from two classes, and make it clear that joining is optional. We won't include names in the report. We thought of noting hand size because it is relevant to the task, but we need a consistent measurement method rather than guessing whether someone's hands are small or large.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: The measuring procedure will be agreed with the tutor beforehand. We also want participants to be able to stop at any point. We shouldn't treat completing every model as a condition of helping us. If a person finds the activity uncomfortable, we'll stop rather than encourage them to continue for the sake of complete data.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. What will your result look like? Be cautious about turning a small set of observations into a precise ranking that appears more certain than your evidence allows.

dialogue.speaker: Leah
dialogue.text: We can make a table of observed actions and summarise comments under themes. A simple total of preferred models might be useful, but it won't replace explaining the reasons. If people prefer different gaps for different reasons, that is a finding we need to preserve rather than average away.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Our final drawing will show a possible revision, with notes explaining which observations influenced it. We'll label it a proposal, not a validated product. Questions about durability, cleaning and actual drinking use would need a different study. Those are outside our current exercise, even if the proposed shape looks convincing.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then do a short rehearsal of the procedure before recruiting the full group. It may show that an instruction is ambiguous or that you can't record two actions at once. Adjust the procedure before the main sessions, and include that adjustment in your method section so the reader can understand how the study developed.

listeningParts.title: Keeping a useful record of material trials
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecturer explains documentation in a supervised craft workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: When makers explore materials, they often produce more small trials than finished objects. A trial may test a surface, a joint or the way two parts fit together. Its value depends partly on being able to connect the result with what was done. A box of attractive fragments can become surprisingly uninformative if nobody remembers which materials or conditions produced them. Today we will consider how a simple recording system can preserve useful information without becoming an obstacle to making.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Begin by giving each trial an identifier. This is not the same as a descriptive title. You might change your description after examining the result, but the identifier should remain stable. Put it on the accompanying record and use it when referring to photographs or notes. If the object itself cannot be marked safely, use an appropriate label or storage position agreed with the workshop supervisor. Do not improvise a marking method that could interfere with the equipment or the trial.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Record the purpose before you begin. A useful purpose is a question that the trial can actually address. 'Find the best surface' is too broad unless best has been defined. Comparing how two prepared samples look under the same light is more specific, although it tells you nothing by itself about their suitability for another use. Writing the question helps prevent an appealing result from being used later as evidence for something that was never investigated.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Next, distinguish the intended procedure from the procedure actually carried out. The plan may specify one material or sequence, while a shortage or an interruption leads to a change. Record the change rather than quietly rewriting the plan to match the result. This is not an admission that the trial has no value. It allows someone else to understand which conditions apply to the observation and decide whether a comparison with another trial is meaningful.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Photographs can help, but include a scale when size matters. A close view may make two very different objects appear similar in dimensions. Also note lighting if appearance is part of the question. An image is a record made under particular conditions, not a complete substitute for the object. Keep the original image available if an edited copy is used in a presentation, and make significant adjustments clear to the reader.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The written result should separate observation from explanation. 'The edge has a visible crack' reports something seen. A claim about why the crack formed is an interpretation that may need further checking. You can record both, provided the distinction remains clear. If another trial is needed to investigate the explanation, state the proposed question. Do not treat a plausible account as settled simply because it fits the first example you noticed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Storage matters too. Keep related records together, or provide links that make the relationship easy to recover. A physical sample in one room and an unexplained photograph in another folder may effectively become two disconnected objects. Decide who will maintain the collection after a course ends. Some trials may be photographed and then discarded under the workshop's normal arrangements, while others remain useful for teaching. The choice should follow a clear purpose rather than happen accidentally.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, preserve evidence of unsuccessful attempts when it helps explain a decision. A collection containing only attractive outcomes can give a misleading picture of an object’s development. This does not mean keeping everything forever. A concise selection, with an explanation of what was removed, can be more useful than an unmanageable archive. The aim is a record that supports accurate reflection: what was attempted, what was observed, what remains uncertain and what a maker might reasonably try next.

readingPassages.title: What a test tile can tell a maker
paragraphs: A small sample can be useful precisely because it is not a finished object. In a supervised pottery workshop, a maker may prepare a test tile to investigate the appearance of a particular surface treatment. The tile allows a limited question to be explored without committing a larger piece to the same process. Yet a successful-looking sample does not answer every question about a future object. The task is to identify what the sample represents, what conditions produced it and which conclusions remain outside its purpose. A useful trial is a source of information, not a miniature guarantee.

The shape of a sample affects how it can be interpreted. A flat tile may show a colour clearly, but a curved object can present that surface differently to the viewer. An edge or a recessed area may create effects absent from a simple flat face. This does not make the tile a poor tool. It means that the maker should choose a sample form suited to the question. If a particular feature of an intended object is important, the trial may need to include an equivalent feature rather than depend on a general resemblance.

Identification is another essential step. A label such as 'blue trial' can become ambiguous when several similar samples exist. A stable code links the object to a record even if its description later changes. The record can state the materials used, the procedure followed and the conditions reported by the workshop supervisor. Where technical operations require specialist control, the maker should not substitute a guessed setting for a missing record. An acknowledged gap in the information is preferable to a precise-looking figure that nobody can verify or explain.

Comparisons become more informative when the variable of interest is separated from other differences. Imagine two samples made with different surface treatments on different underlying bodies. If their appearances differ, the surface treatment alone cannot automatically be credited with the result. The example does not prove that comparison is impossible; it shows why the question and the arrangement must be connected. A maker can either prepare a more controlled comparison or describe the combined change honestly. The least useful response is to overlook the additional difference because it complicates a preferred explanation.

Recording an outcome involves more than deciding whether it is attractive. A note might describe where a colour is uneven, whether an edge appears different from the centre or which features are visible under a stated light. These observations provide a basis for later discussion. The word 'good', on its own, preserves much less information. A result that is unsuitable for one intended appearance might suggest another use, while a visually pleasing result could still require separate investigation before being used in a functional product. Aesthetic judgement and practical suitability are different questions.

Photographs can help makers compare trials when the objects are not together, but they introduce another set of conditions. Lighting, background and the camera's processing can affect the image. Including a reference and keeping the conditions consistent can make a comparison clearer, without turning the photograph into an exact substitute for direct examination. A report should explain whether a description came from viewing the object or its image. Otherwise, a later reader may mistake a photographic difference for a difference in the material itself and pursue an explanation that the evidence does not support.

A collection of samples also needs a policy for keeping and removing items. Retaining every trial can make useful examples difficult to find. Retaining only the most attractive ones can conceal why earlier decisions changed. One practical approach is to keep a selected sequence that explains a particular development, together with notes on what was omitted. The selection should follow its intended use: a teaching collection, a record of a commission and a maker's personal reference library may reasonably contain different things. Completeness is meaningful only in relation to a stated purpose.

Ultimately, the value of a test tile lies in the relationship between an object, a question and a record. None is sufficient by itself. An unexplained object can invite confident speculation; a detailed record without a corresponding sample may be difficult to interpret. Bringing them together allows a maker to identify a reasonable next step while recognising what remains unknown. The most useful sample is therefore not always the most beautiful one. It is one that makes a particular decision better informed and leaves enough evidence for the decision to be reconsidered later.

readingPassages.title: The handle as a relationship
paragraphs: A handle can appear to be a separate part attached after the main object has been designed. For the user, however, it is a point of contact through which the object is approached, supported or moved. Its value depends on a relationship: the hand, the object, the intended action and the circumstances of use. A handle that feels satisfactory in a brief display may behave differently when someone carries the object across a room. Treating it only as a visual detail can therefore leave a central part of the experience unexplored.

The first question is what action the handle supports. Lifting a light empty container is not the same task as controlling it while pouring. Carrying it for a moment differs from holding it during a longer activity. These distinctions matter before dimensions are chosen. An investigation that asks merely whether a handle is comfortable may collect answers to several different imagined tasks. Defining the activity helps participants understand what is being discussed and allows the designer to decide whether the model being used is suitable for that activity at all.

People bring different physical characteristics and learned habits to a task. Even individuals with similar hand dimensions may choose different grips. It is therefore risky to treat one person's preferred arrangement as a universal solution. This does not mean every object needs an unlimited range of handles. It means that a claim about suitability must be linked to the people and activities actually considered. A designer may choose a compromise or provide alternatives, but should not hide the trade-off behind an unsupported assertion that one shape naturally suits everybody.

Early models can answer some questions while remaining inappropriate for others. A lightweight form may allow a person to explore where the fingers fit, yet provide no evidence about carrying a full container. A model made to examine appearance may not be strong enough for any lifting test. The purpose should be stated before someone is asked to handle it, and specialist supervision should determine what use is appropriate. A model is informative when its limits are understood, not when its resemblance to a finished product encourages more confident testing than it can support.

Observation and comment offer different kinds of information. A participant might describe a handle as easy to use while repeatedly changing grip. The discrepancy is a reason to ask a question, not a licence to dismiss the comment. The person may mean that finding a suitable grip was easy, or may be describing an appearance rather than the action just performed. A careful interview allows that meaning to be clarified. Equally, a favourable comment should not erase an observed difficulty simply because it is easier to report a positive verdict.

The order in which alternatives are presented can influence a small trial. A participant may become familiar with the task, compare a model with the immediately preceding example or become tired. Varying order and keeping instructions consistent can help interpret the responses, although neither removes every source of variation. A report should describe the procedure rather than imply that a preference arose independently of it. Results obtained in a classroom exercise can suggest directions for further work without establishing a precise ranking that applies outside the exercise.

Once a form has been selected for further development, other requirements remain. Cleaning, storage, production and the connection between handle and body may raise questions not addressed by the first trial. These requirements can interact. An arrangement that creates more finger space might also occupy more storage space. A designer should explain which conditions were prioritised and what still needs investigation. A successful early comparison is a step in development, not a reason to regard all remaining requirements as minor details that will somehow resolve themselves.

The broader lesson is that a handle should be evaluated through the activity it enables. Measurements, observations and preferences become meaningful when connected to that activity and to the limits of the trial. The goal is not to eliminate judgement from design. It is to make judgement accountable to the evidence available. A reasoned proposal can acknowledge competing needs, justify a choice and identify the next question. In this sense, the apparently small handle reveals something important about product design: a useful object is understood through relationships rather than through isolated dimensions alone.

readingPassages.title: Must a handmade object look imperfect?
paragraphs: A slight irregularity in a handmade object can be valued as a sign of individual work. A bowl may differ from its neighbours, or a line may vary across a surface. Yet it does not follow that irregularity is always desirable, or that a highly consistent object lacks the maker's attention. In my view, the discussion becomes confused when appearance is used as a shortcut for judging a process. The important questions concern what the maker intended, how the object performs and which claims are being made about the relationship between the work and its production.

Consider a set of cups intended to stack in a small cupboard. Differences that prevent stacking may be inconvenient even if each cup is attractive alone. Someone buying a single decorative piece may reasonably have different priorities. I would not describe either preference as inherently more sensitive to craft. The purpose of the purchase changes the relevant judgement. Celebrating every variation as evidence of authenticity ignores the person who needs several objects to work together, while rejecting all variation ignores uses in which difference is part of the appeal.

The word 'imperfection' itself can conceal a decision. A maker may deliberately leave a visible mark, while carefully controlling other dimensions. The resulting object is not necessarily an accidental product that escaped attention. Conversely, an unwanted mark does not become intentional merely because a seller offers a persuasive story about it. Claims of intention should be presented honestly. In my view, buyers are entitled to distinguish a deliberate feature from a problem that the maker did not intend, even when both are visible on the same kind of surface.

Function introduces further distinctions. A variation in colour is different from a defect that affects the intended use. It would be irresponsible to treat every concern as a failure to appreciate handmade work. Where use depends on specialist requirements, those requirements need appropriate assessment rather than a romantic appeal to individuality. This does not reduce a craft object to a technical specification. It recognises that practical reliability and expressive character can both matter, and that a maker should explain the limits of an object rather than expect admiration to replace relevant information.

At the same time, consistency should not be mistaken for the absence of skill. Repeating a form can involve careful attention, and a maker may choose repetition because the objects are intended as a group. I believe the skill lies partly in controlling what matters to the purpose, not simply in producing visible difference. Two pieces that look similar may still reflect individual decisions throughout their making. Judging the entire process from a photograph of their outlines risks overlooking the work required to achieve a chosen relationship between them.

Clear description helps buyers make a choice. A seller can explain expected variation, identify whether the photograph shows the exact object or an example, and distinguish decorative use from other intended uses. Such information need not destroy the pleasure of discovery. It can prevent disappointment arising from an expectation the maker never meant to create. A buyer who receives an object with a different pattern may welcome that difference if it was explained, but feel misled if the image appeared to promise a precise match.

There is also a risk in turning one visual style into a universal sign of authenticity. If every handmade object must display the same kind of irregularity to be recognised as handmade, makers face a new convention rather than freedom from conventions. Some may exaggerate particular marks because those marks are commercially legible. In my view, this is a reason to ask better questions about process, not to suspect every expressive surface. Learning how an object was made can expand appreciation beyond the narrow expectation that honest work must look unfinished.

The sensible conclusion is that neither perfection nor imperfection is a sufficient verdict. The terms need a context: the maker's purpose, the buyer's needs and the consequences of a particular variation. A well-informed choice can value a distinctive mark while expecting the object to perform as described. It can also admire a consistent set without denying the human work behind it. I would favour a conversation based on clear claims and appropriate evidence, rather than a rule requiring every handmade object to demonstrate its origin through a visible irregularity.
